blocking.where: spoke.the-shoreline intro (para 1, sentences 1-2); sections[0].heading and sections[0].body sentence 1; meta_description
blocking.claim: 'Much of the sand at Coney Island Beach was put there by people. The city pumped in 1.7 million cubic yards of sand to widen the beach before the boardwalk opened in 1923.' / 'A large part of Coney Island Beach is man-made.' / meta: 'Much of Coney Island's beach was pumped in by people.'
blocking.problem: The sheet gives only H066: the 'immense engineering project required 1.7 million cubic yards of sand to add another 2.5 million square feet to the beach area'. No fact says the sand was 'pumped'. No fact gives the share of the beach that is man-made, so 'much' and 'a large part' are unsupported. H068 says the 'beach improvement and boardwalk construction began in 1921', so 'before the boardwalk opened in 1923' is also unsupported: the boardwalk opened in stages from Oct 1922 to May 15, 1923 (H064), and no source says the sand work finished first. The page's lede and its search snippet rest on this.
blocking.evidence: https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/coney-island-beach-and-boardwalk/highlights/204 : 'the immense engineering project required 1.7 million cubic yards of sand to add another 2.5 million square feet to the beach area'. Sheet search for pumped/hydraulic/man-made/artificial returns 0 facts.
blocking.fix: intro para 1: 'People added sand to Coney Island Beach to make it wider. A NYC Parks sign says the project that began in 1921 used 1.7 million cubic yards of sand and added 2.5 million square feet of beach. Since then, crews have added more sand and built stone groins, rock structures meant to slow the loss of sand.' | sections[0].heading: 'How did people build the beach?' | sections[0].body first two sentences: 'People added sand to widen Coney Island Beach. The city got title to the beachfront in 1921 and then built the beach out to hold the crowds.' | meta_description: 'People added sand to widen Coney Island's beach. See what Hurricane Sandy took, how the city tests the water, the creek's pollution and the flood plans.'

advisory.claim: 'The 1.2 billion figure is out of line with the record for the species, so this page uses 300 million.'
advisory.problem: Source is only the researcher note in conflicts[50]; no fact id or quote holds either figure, so neither was quote-checked, and the page contradicts an official Parks page in its own voice with no cited source. Parks pages returned 403 to me, so I could not confirm either.
advisory.evidence: conflicts[50]: 'use 300 million (or avoid), and note the 1.2 billion figure is out of line with the species record.'
advisory.fix: 'Two NYC Parks pages disagree on how old the species is. The horseshoe crab page says more than 300 million years. The Coney Island Creek Natural Area page says roughly 1.2 billion years. We could not check either against a science source, so this page does not give an age.'

advisory.claim: 'The raised beach also protected what stood behind it. The Corps estimates that it avoided about $494 million...'
advisory.problem: First sentence states the protection as fact in the page voice; P048/P049 are medium confidence and the figure is the Corps' estimate as quoted by the magazine.
advisory.evidence: P048: 'avoided an estimated $494 million in damages' (Marine Technology Reporter 2023, medium).
advisory.fix: 'The Army Corps says the raised beach limited damage behind it. It estimates that the beach avoided about $494 million in damage to houses and other structures during Sandy. That is the Corps' own estimate, as quoted by Marine Technology Reporter.'

advisory.problem: No fact ranks the city's arguments. P071 also gives durability and non-slip (Parks 'concluded that concrete was more durable than faux wood and didn't get slippery'), and P069 says no suitable wood was found.
advisory.fix: 'The city gave cost and durability as reasons.'

advisory.claim: Heading 'Why is part of the boardwalk concrete and plastic?' (present tense)
advisory.problem: Newest surface fact is Nov 2014 (P074-P076); the body itself says current sections cannot be confirmed, so the heading asserts more than the sheet.
advisory.fix: heading: 'Why did the city replace parts of the boardwalk with concrete and plastic?'; first body sentences: 'The boardwalk was built of wood. After a long public fight, the city approved replacing parts of it with concrete and recycled plastic in 2012.'

advisory.claim: 'Wikipedia puts the boardwalk and related projects at $20 million, a wider scope.'
advisory.problem: 'Wider scope' is inference. H067 says only 'the boardwalk and related improvement projects cost $20 million'; the sign says '$3 million beach improvement and boardwalk construction'. The sheet does not say the two measure different things.
advisory.fix: 'Wikipedia puts the boardwalk and related improvement projects at $20 million. The two figures come from different sources, and we could not reconcile them.'

advisory.claim: 'The new beach did not stay put.'
advisory.problem: Inference. Moses (P019) describes a receding 1937 beach but does not say the 1920s sand washed away.
advisory.fix: 'By 1937 the beach was shrinking.' (then keep the Moses sentence)

advisory.claim: 'Locals still swim, fish and hold religious ceremonies at Kaiser Park on the creek'
advisory.problem: 'Still' presents a Dec 2020 report as current.
advisory.evidence: P095 (Brooklyn Paper, 2020-12): 'many locals use the creek to swim, fish, and conduct religious ceremonies in kaiser park'.
advisory.fix: 'A 2020 Brooklyn Paper report said many locals swim, fish and hold religious ceremonies at Kaiser Park on the creek, which environmentalists say risks long-term harm.'

advisory.claim: 'The Superfund process has moved slowly.' / 'The state does not list a water body unless it is first a federal Superfund site.'
advisory.problem: 'Slowly' is editorial, not in the sheet. The state rule is a Nov 2023 statement given in present tense.
advisory.fix: 'Here is the timeline.' / 'As of November 2023, the state did not list a water body unless it was first a federal Superfund site.'

advisory.claim: 'The biggest flood plan for Coney Island is an Army Corps of Engineers draft...'
advisory.problem: Unsourced superlative; the sheet says only that it is a $52 billion plan 'for New York and parts of New Jersey'.
advisory.fix: 'One major flood plan that includes Coney Island is an Army Corps of Engineers draft called the New York-New Jersey Harbor and Tributaries plan, released September 26, 2022.'

advisory.claim: 'The city Health Department tests the water at Coney Island every week during beach season. Sampling starts one month before the season opens.'
advisory.problem: Time-sensitive rule (V047/V048, 2026) carries no year, and the 2026 season ended Sept 13.
advisory.fix: 'In 2026 the city Health Department tested the water at Coney Island every week during beach season. Sampling started one month before the season opened.'

advisory.claim: 'On July 9 the city warned people to stay out of the water at a dozen beaches.'
advisory.problem: Counts differ by outlet: ABC7 says 'a dozen' (V053, confirmed on the page), Fox says 18 locations were under advisory (V058). The page does not attribute.
advisory.fix: 'On July 9, ABC7 reported the city warned people to stay out of the water at a dozen beaches. Fox Weather counted 18 locations under advisory.'
